title: Iran War's Retail Toll Is Uneven, but It Adds Up to About $2,000 a Household
excerpt: Seven months in, fuel and airfares carry the clearest price rises, groceries and shoes are moving slower, and wholesale and freight costs point to more pressure ahead of the midterms.
body:
• Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi estimates the Iran war has cost the average US household almost $2,000: $1,100 in energy, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs, with energy still rising $50 a week.
  • Gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon on Friday, 45% above the $2.98 prewar level, and diesel was $6.33, up 68% from $3.76, according to AAA figures reported by the Associated Press.
  • For households budgeting now: airfares were about 22% higher in September than a year earlier, and parcel carriers levy fuel surcharges on top of an 8% US Postal Service price rise in April.
  • Groceries and shoes have risen more slowly, but a September jump in wholesale prices warns that more costs may still reach store shelves.

Seven months into the US war with Iran, the bill for American households is uneven but cumulative, according to an Associated Press review of retail prices. Fuel and air travel carry the clearest increases; most store goods have moved far less, because companies have absorbed part of their higher costs — a cushion the AP says may not last if fuel stays elevated into the midterms.

Fuel Is Where the War Shows Up First

Before the war, regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76, according to AAA. Gasoline peaked at $4.56 in May; diesel reached a record $6.53 in September. On Friday the averages were $4.33 and $6.33. The AP noted this is the first October in which regular gasoline has averaged more than $4. Diesel matters beyond the pump: it moves freight, so its 68% rise feeds the cost of almost everything shipped. The Energy Information Administration expects winter heating costs to be 21% higher for households that heat with oil.

Flying Costs More, and Capacity Is Thinner

Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September, according to International Air Transport Association figures cited by the AP. Airlines have raised prices and fees and trimmed schedules. Airfares were about 22% higher in September than a year earlier in the consumer price index, and average domestic fares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April-June quarter, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. For US diaspora families planning winter travel, that fare pressure is likely to reach their budgets first.

Groceries Have Moved Less Than the Inputs Behind Them

The Agriculture Department initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year; it now expects 2.4%. The inputs behind food have risen much faster: the USDA revised 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops up by 9% to 13%, and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates up by 33% to 41%. Cornell economist Chris Barrett told the AP retailers appear to be absorbing increases after years of food inflation. Fresh produce is most exposed next, as it depends on trucking and refrigeration.

Shoes and Shipping Show the Slower Pass-Through

Roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September than a year earlier, with men's shoes up 4.5%.

"Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers."

— Matt Priest, President and CEO, Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America

September producer-price data showed transportation and warehousing costs up 10.2% year on year, with truck and water freight each up 19.3%. The Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April, and UPS, FedEx and DHL impose fuel surcharges. AFS Logistics and TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter.

Other Estimates Land in the Same Range

Moody's updated tally, reported by CNN as about $265 billion in total consumer costs, has climbed from the roughly $1,760 per household Zandi calculated in September, covered by The Videshi in our earlier report on the war's oil and rates squeeze. A tally at the American Enterprise Institute put the cost through September 21 at about $1,380 per household, rising to around $2,000 with Moody's interest-rate estimate added. CNN also reported wage growth slowed in September to a five-year low. The White House disputed Zandi's record and defended the war's objective of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

What Households Should Watch Next

What decides whether the impact widens is whether the September wholesale-price jump reaches store prices, and whether holiday parcel rates set records as projected. The AP's conclusion is narrow: increases so far are concentrated in fuel, fares and shipping, companies are still absorbing part of the rest, and that absorption — not the underlying costs — is what has kept store prices from rising across the board.
